title: An online shop for a jewelry studio
metaTitle: A jewelry shop for detail and size
excerpt: A jewelry studio shop has to show detail, size, and how the object is cared for. Then keep checkout short. A marketplace grid will not carry the piece.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops, planning how a jewelry piece will be explained.
caption: A workshop table where the facts of a piece get named. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a jewelry product page show first?
faqs.answer: Show the piece large, then the name, the price, the metal, and the size choice if there is one. Add how it was made, how to care for it, and the lead time if it is not ready to ship. A way to ask about that specific piece should sit with the buy button.

faqs.question: How do you explain jewelry size online?
faqs.answer: Pair a consistent scale photograph with a measurement in type. Rings need a sizing method you trust, and a clear note if you cannot resize that construction. Earrings should mention weight when it will matter after an hour of wear.

faqs.question: Should a jewelry studio require an account at checkout?
faqs.answer: Let people pay as a guest, and show the full total, including shipping, before the card. You can offer an account after the receipt for people who want the care notes saved. A forced account and a late total are common reasons a considered order stops.

markdown:
A jewelry studio ecommerce website has to show the object closely enough that a person can judge it. Detail, size, and the care in how it was made are the page. Checkout comes after those are clear, and it should stay short. A marketplace grid of tiny tiles and star ratings will not carry a piece someone wears on their body.

The shop can be small. A studio with forty pieces does not need the furniture of a catalog with forty thousand. It needs a page that tells the truth about metal, scale, and what happens if the piece must be repaired or resized.

## Detail is the decision

People buy studio jewelry with their eyes, then with a few facts. The photograph has to survive being opened full screen. The page has to name what the photograph cannot prove.

Put these facts next to the picture, in the first screen:

- Metal, and the purity or plating if that distinction changes the price or the care.
- Stones, if any, in plain language. Say if they are lab-grown, recycled, or a stand-in you will swap.
- Dimensions that matter: inner length, width of a band, drop of an earring.
- What is included: the chain, the box, the pouch, nothing extra.

"Handmade" is not a fact by itself. If you fabricate in the studio, say what you do: cast, set, finish, or assemble. If a component comes from a supplier, you can still be a studio. Say which part is yours. Collectors and careful gifters both notice the difference, and a vague line reads as a costume.

Hallmarks, maker's marks, and edition size belong on the page when they exist. If the piece is one of one, say one of one, and remove the buy button when it sells. If you will make it again to order, say the lead time in weeks you have actually hit, not a hopeful number from a quiet month.

Do not hide the price. A studio can be expensive and still print the number. "Price on request" is reasonable for a commission with a wide range. It is a poor default for a ring you have already made and photographed. The people who cannot afford it will leave either way. The people who can will not enjoy a scavenger hunt.

## Size has to be legible

Size is the most common disappointment in online jewelry, and it is mostly a design problem. A macro crop makes a delicate stud look like a brooch. The page has to give scale in more than one way.

Show the piece on a body or in a hand you use consistently, and give a measurement in type. Both. The photograph convinces. The number confirms. "About the width of a grain of rice" helps, and it does not replace millimeters when a person is comparing two bands.

Rings need a way to choose a size without a comedy of errors. Publish the method you trust: a printable guide, a string method you have tested, or a note to measure a ring they already wear. If you offer one free resize, say the window and the sizes you can reach. If you do not resize a particular construction, say that on the piece, not in a policy footer nobody opens.

Earrings need a note on weight. A beautiful drop that hurts after an hour will come back. Weight in grams, and a line about whether it suits a long dinner, is care. It is also fewer returns.

Chains and necklaces need length on a person, not only in centimeters. Two lengths, photographed the same way, beat a dropdown that says 40 cm and 45 cm to a buyer who does not think in centimeters. You can keep the numbers. Add the picture.

## Care is a fact

Care is how the object will live, not a mood. Write the care you will stand behind.

If the piece should be taken off to swim, sleep, or shower, say so in a sentence. If the finish will change and you consider that part of the metal, say that too. A studio that sells recycled silver can talk about tarnish as an honest property. A studio that promises a forever polish and then writes a twelve-step regimen has made a different promise. Pick one.

Repair and resizing are part of the sale for work at this level. Say whether you repair what you made, what it costs in broad terms if you know, and how to start: a form, a visit, a booked time. "We stand behind our work" without a path is a slogan. A path is an address and a person.

Packaging can be one line and one picture of the closed box or the pouch, if it is part of the gift. Do not let the box become the product. The piece is the product. The box is how it arrives.

Certificates and receipts should be mentioned if you provide them. If you do not provide a gemological certificate, do not imply one with a badge. Inventing paperwork is worse than a plain description.

## The piece page

Order the page so a skeptical person can decide without a phone call, and a person who wants a call can still ask.

1. The piece, large, with a way to see detail.
2. Name, price, metal, and the size choice if there is one.
3. Three or four sentences on how it was made and how to care for it.
4. Lead time, if it is not shipping from a drawer.
5. A way to ask a question about this piece, with the name already attached.
6. The button to buy, or the button to commission, if those are different paths.

Commissions are not ready-made stock. Give them a separate form: budget, date, a description, and whether they have a size. Do not send a commission through the same checkout as a finished band unless the deposit logic is something you have actually built and tested. A deposit that fails is a broken relationship, not a theme setting.

Related pieces should be other work from the studio, chosen, in small number. If you only have a few objects, show them. Do not fill the row with "you may also like" from an algorithm that has no taste yet. An empty recommendation row is a marketplace habit. Leave it out until a human can name the neighbors.

Page titles should name the piece and the metal. A title that says "Shop" on every object helps no one recognize the page in a search result or a forwarded link. The person who receives the link is often buying a gift and will not call you to ask which ring this was.

## Checkout for a considered purchase

The person paying for a piece of jewelry is already slightly tense. The checkout should not add reasons to leave.

[Baymard Institute](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) finds that 19 percent of abandoning US shoppers did not trust the site with a credit card, and 18 percent left because the site wanted an account. Twelve percent could not see the total up front. A studio order is a considered one. It still dies on trust, on a forced registration, and on a surprise total.

Show the total, including shipping and any duty you know, before you ask for the card. If you ship insured, say the insurance is included or show the fee. Quiet insurance is good. A fee that appears at the end feels like a trick, even when it is reasonable.

Guest checkout should be available. Offer an account afterward for people who want the receipt and the care notes in one place. The care notes also belong in the confirmation email, because that is the document they will keep.

Use a payment provider you can speak about plainly. A known method, a visible total, and an address that matches the studio name do more for trust than a row of badges. If you have not done a security certification, do not invent a seal. Honesty is the trust signal a small studio can actually own.

Confirmation should repeat what they bought, the size, the lead time, and how to ask a question. A person who ordered a resize will reread that page. Write it as if they will.

## A studio is not a marketplace tile

Marketplace pages are built to compare many sellers of a similar thing. Your page is built to explain one object. Tiny thumbnails, review stars from strangers, and a seller rating are the wrong tools.

Show fewer pieces, larger. If the studio's range is small, the homepage can be the range. A grid is fine when the crop is consistent and the tiles are big enough to read a silhouette. It is a failure when every piece is a sparkle in the corner of a lifestyle scene and the metal is a guess.

Filters are useful for metal, type of object, and availability: ready, or made to order. Filters for every aesthetic adjective are a blog, not a shop. "Minimal," "bold," and "everyday" can be a sentence you write. They do not need to be facets on day one.

Discount timers and low-stock panic are a poor fit for work you want people to keep. If a piece is the last one, you can say "one made." Say it once, in type, next to the facts.

The photographs have to do the quiet part of this work: detail, scale, and the sense that the object was handled carefully. That is its own practice, and it is the next piece: [product photography for a jewelry studio](/blog/product-photography-for-a-jewelry-studio).
